# Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem {#sec-hydro}

## The virial theorem

We consider a self-gravitating cloud of gas in equilibrium, described by the momentum equation
$$
\frac{\partial (\rho \vb{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] = - \rho \nabla \Psi,
$$ {#eq-hydro-1}
where $\Psi$ is the gravitational potential. We consider the scalar moment of inertia[^hydro-1]
$$
I = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \rho (\vb{r}) r^2 \dd V,
$$ {#eq-hydro-2}
where $V$ is a volume that encloses the whole gas cloud. The time derivative of $I$ is (using the continuity equation)
$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\frac{\dd I}{\dd t} &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \frac{\partial
\rho}{\partial t} r^2 \dd V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho
\vb{v}) r^2 \dd V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \vb{v}r^2) \dd V +
\frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \nabla r^2 \dd V.
\end{alignedat}
$$ {#eq-hydro-3}
The total divergence term is equal to a boundary integral
$$
\int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \vb{v}r^2) \dd V = \int_S \rho
\vb{v}r^2 \cdot \vb{n} \dd S,
$$ {#eq-hydro-4}
but the latter vanishes since, by assumption, $\rho \rightarrow 0$ at the boundary of $V$. So we find
$$
\frac{\dd I}{\dd t} = \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \nabla
r^2 \dd V = \int_V \rho \vb{v} \cdot \vb{r} \dd V.
$$ {#eq-hydro-5}
Here, we have used the fact that $\nabla r =\vb{r}/ r$.

The second time derivative of $I$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\dd^2 I}{\dd t^2} &= \int_V \frac{\partial (\rho \vb{v})}{\partial t} \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] \cdot \vb{r} \dd V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd V - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho (\vb{v} \cdot \vb{r}) \vb{v}+ p\vb{r}] \dd V \\
&\qquad + \int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r} \dd V.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-6}
Where the notation $\vb{A}: \vb{B}$ denotes the inner product between two tensors:
$$
\vb{A}: \vb{B}= \sum_{i = 1}^3 \sum_{k = 1}^3 A_{i k} B_{k i} =
\operatorname{Trace} \left[ \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
A_{x x} & A_{x y} & A_{x z}\\
A_{y x} & A_{y y} & A_{y z}\\
A_{z x} & A_{z y} & A_{z z}
\end{array}\right)  \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
B_{x x} & B_{x y} & B_{x z}\\
B_{y x} & B_{y y} & B_{y z}\\
B_{z x} & B_{z y} & B_{z z}
\end{array}\right) \right] .
$$ {#eq-hydro-7}
Once again, we can drop the total divergence terms, since they vanish due to Gauss' theorem, to find
$$
\frac{\dd^2 I}{\dd t^2} = - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot
\vb{r} \dd V + \int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+
p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r} \dd V.
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-base}
The second term in the RHS is simpler than it looks, because
$$
\nabla \vb{r}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x x & \partial_x y & \partial_x z\\
\partial_y x & \partial_y y & \partial_y z\\
\partial_z x & \partial_z y & \partial_z z
\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right) =\vb{I}.
$$ {#eq-hydro-9}
So everything simplifies to
$$
\int_V [\rho \vb{v} \otimes \vb{v}+ p\vb{I}] : \nabla \vb{r}
\dd V = \int_V \rho v^2 \dd V + 3 \int_V p \dd V =: 2 T +
3 \Pi,
$$ {#eq-hydro-10}
where $T$ is the kinetic energy of the gas and $\Pi$ is the integrated pressure.

The first term in the RHS of @eq-hydro-virial-base requires a little more work. First, we need to compute an expression for the gravitational potential in terms of the mass density $\rho$. To do this, we remember that the gravitational potential generated by a distribution of point masses with mass $m_i$ at locations $\vb{r}_i$ is given by
$$
\Psi (\vb{r}) = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{Gm_i}{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}_i
|} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-11}
This can be generalized to the case of a mass density distribution by converting the sum into an integral
$$
\Psi (\vb{r}) = - \int_V \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}')}{ |
\vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \dd \vb{r}' .
$$ {#eq-hydro-12}
Inserting this into the first term in the RHS of @eq-hydro-virial-base yields
$$
\int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd \vb{r} = - \int_V
\dd \vb{r} \rho (\vb{r}) \nabla_{\vb{r}} \int_V \dd
\vb{r}'  \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}')}{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \cdot
\vb{r},
$$ {#eq-hydro-derivative-of-potential}
where we have used the notation $\nabla_{\vb{r}}$ to remind ourselves that the derivatives are computed with respect to the unprimed position $\vb{r}$. In particular, note that $\rho (\vb{r}')$ in the integral is not affected by the derivative, since it is a function of $\vb{r}'$ and not of $\vb{r}$. The only term that we need to differentiate is the denominator:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla_{\vb{r}} \frac{1}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \\
& \quad = \nabla_{\vb{r}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2}} \\
& \quad = \frac{- 1}{[(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2]^{3 / 2}} \\
& \qquad\quad \times \left(\begin{array}{c}
x - x' \\
y - y' \\
z - z'
\end{array}\right) \\
& \quad = - \frac{\vb{r}-\vb{r}'}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-diff-one-over-r}
Inserting the last expression into @eq-hydro-derivative-of-potential, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd \vb{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd \vb{r} \int_V \dd \vb{r}' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd \vb{r} \int_V \dd \vb{r}' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \\
& \qquad\qquad + \int_V \dd \vb{r} \int_V \dd \vb{r}' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r}' \\
& \quad = \int_V \dd \vb{r} \int_V \dd \vb{r}' \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}') \rho (\vb{r}) }{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} \\
& \qquad + \int_V \dd \vb{r}' \rho (\vb{r}') \int_V \dd \vb{r} \frac{G \rho (\vb{r}) }{ | \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} (\vb{r}-\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r}' \\
& \quad = - \int_V \dd \vb{r} \Psi (\vb{r}) \rho (\vb{r}) - \int_V \rho (\vb{r}') \nabla_{\vb{r}'} \Psi (\vb{r}') \cdot \vb{r}' \dd \vb{r}' .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hydro-expansion-of-grad-potential}
We have used the fact that (note the difference in sign compared to @eq-hydro-diff-one-over-r)
$$
\nabla_{\vb{r}'}  \frac{1}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |} =
\frac{\vb{r}-\vb{r}'}{| \vb{r}-\vb{r}' |^3} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-16}
The last term on the RHS of @eq-hydro-expansion-of-grad-potential is identical to the LHS, so we find
$$
- \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \vb{r} \dd \vb{r}= \frac{1}{2}
\int_V \dd \vb{r} \Psi (\vb{r}) \rho (\vb{r}) = \Omega,
$$ {#eq-hydro-17}
$\Omega$ being the gravitational potential energy.

For a **stationary configuration** $\dd^2 I / \dd t^2 = 0$, so @eq-hydro-virial-base yields the *virial theorem*:
$$
\boxed{\Omega + 2 T + 3 \Pi = 0.}
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-theorem}
For an ideal gas $p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon$, so
$$
\Pi = \int_V p \dd V = (\Gamma - 1) \int_V \rho \varepsilon \dd V =
(\Gamma - 1) U,
$$ {#eq-hydro-19}
where $U$ is the total internal energy. In this case, the virial theorem reads
$$
\boxed{\Omega + 2 T + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.}
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-ideal-gas}

## Hydrostatic equilibria

The virial theorem has an important consequence for the stability of hydrostatic equilibria. Consider a cloud of gas or star in hydrostatic equilibrium, that is with no large scale motion (no rotation). Then the virial theorem states that
$$
\Omega + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
$$ {#eq-hydro-virial-simple}
On the other hand, the energy of the cloud is
$$
E = \Omega + U.
$$ {#eq-hydro-energy}
The energy must be negative for the system to be stable $E \leq 0$. This implies
$$
U \leq - \Omega = 3 (\Gamma - 1) U \Longrightarrow [- 1 + 3 (\Gamma -
1)] U \geq 0,
$$ {#eq-hydro-23}
since $U \geq 0$, this requires
$$
\Gamma \geq 4 / 3.
$$ {#eq-hydro-24}
Monoatomic gas has $\Gamma = 5 / 3$, so regular stars are stable. White dwarfs close to their maximum mass and very hot stars that are radiation pressure dominated have $\Gamma \approx 4 / 3$, so they are unstable. They explode as Type Ia supernovae and pair-instability supernova, respectively.

A surprising consequence of the virial theorem is that self-gravitating systems have *negative specific heat*. Consider a self-gravitating cloud (a protostar) emitting infrared radiation. As its energy $E$ becomes more negative its gravitational binding energy $- \Omega$ must increase, because $U \geq 0$. We can use @eq-hydro-virial-simple and @eq-hydro-energy to solve for $U$ in terms of $E$:
$$
U = - \frac{E}{3 \Gamma - 4} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-internal-energy-from-virial}
If $\Gamma > 4 / 3$, @eq-hydro-internal-energy-from-virial predicts that $U$ will increase as $E$ becomes more negative. Meaning that the system heats up as it loses energy! Eventually the cloud contracts to the point that nuclear fusion starts occurring and a star is born. Nuclear burning *prevents* the star from heating up further.

## Application to star formation

Consider a spherical cloud of radius $R$. Let the typical density be $\bar{\rho}$. Then the gravitational potential energy is (neglecting factors of order unity)
$$
- \Omega = G \int_0^R 4 \pi r \rho (r) \mathcal{M} (r) \dd r \approx (4
\pi)^2 G \bar{\rho}^2 R^5,
$$ {#eq-hydro-26}
where
$$
\mathcal{M} (r) = \int_0^r 4 \pi r^2 \rho (r) \dd r.
$$ {#eq-hydro-27}
For an ideal gas, the pressure is given by
$$
p = \frac{k_B T}{Am_p} \rho,
$$ {#eq-hydro-28}
where $A$ is the atomic mass unit of the gas in units of the proton mass $m_p$, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the temperature. We can assume $T$ to be constant. This is a good approximation for optically thin clouds which can efficiently cool by emitting radiation. With this approximation
$$
\Pi = \int_0^R 4 \pi r^2 p (r) \dd r \approx \frac{4}{3} \pi c_s^2
\bar{\rho} R^3,
$$ {#eq-hydro-29}
where
$$
c_s^2 = \frac{k_B T}{Am_p}
$$ {#eq-hydro-30}
is a constant. As we will see later, $c_s$ turns out to be the sound speed of the gas. The condition for collapse of the cloud is that $3 \Pi < | \Omega |$, which implies that collapse will occur for a cloud with
$$
R > R_J, \qquad R_J^2 = \frac{c_s^2}{4 \pi \bar{\rho} G} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-31}
This is called the *Jeans length*. Typical molecular clouds have $R \gg R_J$. So instead of collapsing to an object with mass equal to the mass of the cloud, they fragment into smaller stars. The mass of these protostars can be estimated as the mass contained within one Jeans radius, the so-called *Jeans mass*[^hydro-2]:
$$
M_J = \frac{4 \pi}{3}  \bar{\rho} R_J^3 = \frac{c_s^3}{3 (4 \pi
\bar{\rho})^{1 / 2} G^{3 / 2}} = \frac{k_B^{3 / 2}}{3 (4 \pi)^{1 / 2} m_p^2
G^{3 / 2}}  \frac{T^{3 / 2}}{A^2 n^{1 / 2}} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-32}
In CGS units the Jeans mass is
$$
M_J \approx 1.59 M_{\odot}  \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{3 / 2}
\left( \frac{\operatorname{cm}^{- 3}}{n} \right)^{1 / 2}  \frac{1}{A^2} .
$$ {#eq-hydro-jeans-mass}
For a typical molecular cloud with $T = 10\,\mathrm{K}$, $n = 100 \operatorname{cm}^{- 3}$, and $A = 2$ (for molecular hydrogen) the Jeans mass is $M_J \approx 1.25 M_{\odot}$, giving a reasonable estimate for the typical mass of a fragment of the cloud. Note however that the Jeans mass decreases with increasing $n$, so, if the gas can efficiently cool, the cloud might undergo further fragmentation forming clusters of small stars.

While the arguments we have given here give an order of magnitude estimate for the mass of protostars, star formation is strongly influenced by a number of factors that we have neglected. These include turbulence and magnetic fields. Moreover, star formation strongly depends on the ability of the gas to cool to low temperature, as shown by @eq-hydro-jeans-mass.

## In-class worksheet {#sec-hydro-worksheet}

For a magnetic star the virial theorem becomes:
$$
\Omega + 2 T + 3 \Pi +\mathfrak{M}= 0,
$$ {#eq-hydro-ws1}
where the new term is the magnetic energy of the star, which is (in CGS units)
$$
\mathfrak{M}= \frac{1}{8 \pi} \int B^2 \dd V,
$$ {#eq-hydro-ws2}

1.  Find the condition for stability of a nonrotating star in terms of $\Gamma$ and $\mathfrak{M}$.

2.  What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a Solar type star ($R = 7 \cdot 10^6 \operatorname{km}, M = 2 \cdot 10^{33} \mathrm{g}$)?

3.  What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a neutron star ($R = 12 \operatorname{km}$, $M = 3 \cdot 10^{33} \mathrm{g}$)?

## Exercises {#sec-hydro-exercises}

::: {#exr-hydro-slab}
## Self-gravitating slab

An infinite, static slab of incompressible fluid with uniform density $\rho_0$ fills the region $| z | < a$ and is held together by its own gravity.

1.  Compute the gravitational acceleration inside and outside the slab, and the pressure profile inside it.

2.  Model the disk of a galaxy as such a slab, with $\rho_0 = 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and $a = 10^{20}\,\mathrm{cm}$. A star starts at rest at $z = a$. How fast does it cross the mid-plane, and what is the period of its vertical oscillation?

Adapted from @clarke2007, Problem 8.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
1.  The Poisson equation reads
    $$
    \partial_z^2 \Psi (z) = 4 \pi G \rho (z) .
    $$
    By symmetry, we can assume $\partial_z \Psi (0) = 0$. We can then integrate the Poisson equation to find
    $$
    \partial_z \Psi (z) = 4 \pi G \int_0^z \rho (z) \dd z = 4 \pi G \rho_0
    \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z, & z < a,\\
    a, & z \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    Since the potential is unique up to a constant, we can also set $\Psi (0) = 0$. A second integration of Poisson equation then yields
    $$
    \Psi (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z^2, & z < a,\\
    a (2 z - a), & z \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    Using the symmetry of the problem we conclude that
    $$
    \Psi (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    z^2, & | z | < a,\\
    a (2 | z | - a), & | z | \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$
    The momentum equation reads
    $$
    \rho \frac{\dd \vb{v}}{\dd t} = - \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi .
    $$
    For $| z | < a$ this implies that
    $$
    p = - \rho_0 \Psi + \operatorname{const} .
    $$
    The integration constant can be found from the requirement that $p (a) = 0$:
    $$
    0 = p (a) = - 2 \pi G \rho_0^2 a^2 + \operatorname{const} \Longrightarrow
    \operatorname{const} = 2 \pi G \rho_0^2 a^2 .
    $$
    So the pressure is
    $$
    p (z) = 2 \pi G \rho_0^2  \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    a^2 - z^2, & | z | < a,\\
    0, & | z | \geq a.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$

2.  The equation of motion for a star in the region $| z | \leq a$ is:
    $$
    \ddot{z} (t) = - \partial_z \Psi = - 4 \pi G \rho_0 z = : - \omega^2 z.
    $$
    The general solution is
    $$
    z (t) = A \sin (\omega t) + B \cos (\omega t) .
    $$
    Let's assume that at $t = 0$ the star is passing through the galaxy mid plane ($z (0) = 0$), then the solution is
    $$
    z (t) = A \sin (\omega t) .
    $$
    We are told that the maximum distance traveled vertically by the star is $a$, so $A = a$. The velocity of the star at the moment it is passing through $z = 0$ is then
    $$
    \dot{z} (0) = [a \omega \cos (\omega t)]_{t = 0} = a \omega \approx 30
    \operatorname{km} \mathrm{s}^{- 1} .
    $$
    The period of the oscillation is
    $$
    \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} = \frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{4 \pi G \rho_0}} \approx 7 \operatorname{Myr} .
    $$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-cloud}
## Mass of a molecular cloud

A self-gravitating cloud of molecular hydrogen $\left( p = nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} \rho \varepsilon \right)$ is measured to have radius $R = 0.1 \operatorname{pc}$ and temperature $T = 10\mathrm{K}$. *Estimate* the mass of the cloud.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
We can use the virial theorem:
$$
\Omega + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
$$
Assuming the cloud to be spherical and constant density, we have
$$
\Omega = - \frac{3}{5}  \frac{GM^2}{R} .
$$
From the equation of state we have
$$
nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} n \mu \varepsilon \Longrightarrow \varepsilon =
\frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu}
$$
The energy content of the cloud is given by
$$
U = \int u \dd V = \int \rho \varepsilon \dd V = \int \rho
\frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu} \dd V = \frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu}
\int \rho \dd V = \frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{\mu} M.
$$
So we have ($\Gamma = 7 / 5$, $\mu = 2 m_p$)
$$
- \frac{3}{5}  \frac{GM^2}{R} + 3 k_B T \frac{M}{\mu} = 0 \Longrightarrow M
= \frac{5}{2}  \frac{k_B T}{Gm_p} R = 4.81 M_{\odot} .
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-sun}
## Temperature of the solar core

Estimate the temperature at the centre of the Sun, assuming that density and pressure change over a length scale comparable to the solar radius. Make the estimate twice: first assuming that the Sun is supported by gas pressure, then assuming that it is supported by radiation pressure. Which assumption is more plausible, and why?

Adapted from @clarke2007, Problem 11.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
We assume that the density profile of the Sun is given by
$$
\rho (r) = \rho_0  \left( 1 - \frac{r}{R_{\odot}} \right) .
$$
We fix $\rho_0$ by asking that
$$
M_{\odot} = 4 \pi \int_0^{R_{\odot}} \rho (r) r^2 \dd r = \frac{\pi}{3}
R_{\odot}^3 \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 = \frac{3 M_{\odot}}{\pi
R_{\odot}^3} \approx \frac{M_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3} .
$$
Similarly, we assume that the pressure is given by
$$
p (r) = p_0  \left( 1 - \frac{r}{R_{\odot}} \right) .
$$
The hydrostatic equilibrium condition is
$$
\partial_r p = - \frac{p_0}{R_{\odot}} = - \frac{GM}{r^2} \rho \approx
\frac{GM}{R_{\odot}^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow p_0 = \frac{GM_{\odot}
\rho_0}{R_{\odot}} .
$$
If the Sun is supported by gas pressure, we can estimate its core temperature with the ideal-gas law. Approximating the mean molecular weight to be $\mu = \frac{1}{2} m_p$, we find
$$
\frac{\rho_0}{\frac{1}{2} m_p} k_B T = p_0 = \frac{GM_{\odot}
\rho_0}{R_{\odot}} \Longrightarrow k_B T = \frac{1}{2}  \frac{m_p
GM_{\odot} }{R_{\odot}} \approx 10^7 \mathrm{K}.
$$
If the pressure is provided by radiation pressure, then we would have
$$
T = \left( \frac{3 GM_{\odot} \rho_0}{aR_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 4} = \left(
\frac{3 GM_{\odot}^2}{aR_{\odot}^4} \right)^{1 / 4} \approx 4.6 \cdot 10^7
\mathrm{K}.
$$
Because gas pressure becomes dominant at lower temperatures, we conclude that it is more likely for the Sun to be supported by gas pressure.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-hydro-lane-emden}
## Numerical solution of the Lane–Emden equation

Write a code to compute numerically the solution of the Lane–Emden equation for a given $n$.

1.  Validate your code by comparing numerical and analytic solution for $n = 0, 1, 5$.

2.  Plot the solution for $n = 1.5$ and find the radius of the polytrope, i.e., the value $\xi_r$ at which $\theta (\xi_r) = 0$.

*Hint:* use the `solve_ivp` function from `scipy.integrate`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
To use `solve_ivp`, we need to convert the Lane–Emden equation into a system of first order equations. This is accomplished by introducing a new variable $\varphi$ such that
$$
\frac{\dd \theta}{\dd \xi} = \varphi, \qquad \frac{\dd
\varphi}{\dd \xi} = - \frac{2 \varphi}{\xi} - \theta^n .
$$
The boundary conditions are $\theta (\xi = 0) = 1$ and
$$
\lim_{\xi \rightarrow 0^+} \frac{\varphi}{\xi} = 0.
$$
The latter condition comes from the requirement that $\theta$ should be an even function of $\xi$ (for symmetry).

See [`lane-emden.py`](https://github.com/dradice/astrofluids/blob/main/solutions/code/hydrostatic-equilibrium/lane-emden.py) for the implementation.
:::
:::

[^hydro-1]: Sometimes called the virial.

[^hydro-2]: Note that this definition is slightly different from the one given in @clarke2007; however, this difference is inconsequential given the level of approximation of these arguments.
